title: Ballads, race records and Hall's protest about the label
summary: Discussion of what Black bands were allowed to record and Hall's request to labels about race records.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, two things that you were talking about raised questions in my mind or comments in my mind. You were talking about the auditions and having to play all hot tunes, because rereading Rex Stewart's book, and he talked about Fletcher's band and how they had all these great waltz things and these medleys. He had a whole rose medley in which he did 'Roses of Picardy' and all these beautiful things, and they'd never let them record those.
No, not even the small bands.

Yeah. But yet there was -- then there was the whole tradition of the ballad that was -- you know, Coleman Hawkins with 'Body and Soul' and -- so those were recorded. Those became popular, and that was, you know, what you might call slower, sweeter music, even though it was improvised. You'd get to the people on a certain level.
Well, when Coleman recorded 'Body and Soul,' musicians were just coming downtown to the studios. We weren't recording at all except for rhythm and blues Decca.
Yeah, the Sepia Series, as they called it then.
Yeah. And Race Records, they were called.
It's all -- when I started Wax Records, I went around to the different record companies to ask them to -- not to use that label, which didn't make me popular at all.
